title: Use video of man's intoxication death as a training tool: inquiry
article: Surveillance video of a severely intoxicated man who died in RCMP custody should be used to train other officers, according to recommendations from an inquiry into the man's death.

A report on the public fatality inquiry into Sylvester Omeasoo's death was released Mon-day. The 47-year-old Hobbema man died in his cell at the Wetaskiwin RCMP detachment on Oct. 6, 2008, about 90 minutes after being arrested in a liquor store parking lot for public intoxication. An autopsy concluded he died of acute alcohol poisoning. The report found officers did nothing to cause or contribute to his death.

"There is every reason to believe Mr. Omea-soo would have died that night of ethanol toxicity had (the arresting officer) never seen him in the parking lot," read the report from provincial court Judge William Andreassen.

Surveillance video that showed Omeasoo as he was brought into the detachment and searched by officers, and while he was in his cell, was submitted as evidence in the inquiry. Andreassen recommended it be edited and used to train officers on how to assess intoxicated prisoners.
RCMP policy states that officers must seek medical assistance for people who cannot walk, talk or be roused and that the responsiveness of people in custody should be checked often.

The RCMP also investigated Omeasoo's death and found that while he was responsive at the time of arrest, his condition quickly deteriorated. That investigation concluded that Omeasoo's inability to control his neck and failure to protect his head while he was being processed was a sign that he was no longer in control of himself.
Andreassen's report agreed with that conclusion and recommended that specific video footage be shown in officer training.
The report also recommended a review of how often RCMP conduct visual checks of holding cells and said the installation of emergency buttons in cells be considered.
Spokesman Sgt. Tim Taniguchi said the recommendations will be reviewed by RCMP at the national and local levels.

The report states that alcohol abuse is a serious problem in Wetaskiwin, and it's not un-usual for people to drink hairspray, Listerine or even paint thinner. The officer who arrested Omeasoo testified that he arrests as many as five people for public intoxication per shift.

Omeasoo smelled strongly of alcohol when he was arrested; a three-quarter full bottle of hairspray was sitting next to him. He had been arrested for public intoxication more than 40 times in the two years before he died.

The autopsy determined that Omeasoo's blood-alcohol concentration was 0.52 when he died, more than six times the legal driving limit. Dr. Graeme Jones, chief toxicologist with the Alberta Medical Examiners' office, testified that alcohol concentration becomes potentially fatal between 0.35 and 0.40.
Jones was not able to say if Omeasoo would have survived had he been taken directly to hospital from the parking lot.
